column4: This ayah gathers the section's whole scene in one ruling: al-maysir, al-ansab, and al-azlam are filth from Satan's work.
It directly forbids both an animal slaughtered on al-nusub and seeking an allotted division with al-azlam, joining the bloodied stone to the arrows that assign portions.
The answer about al-maysir acknowledges human benefits but declares its sin greater, supplying the moral judgment on the apparently profitable division described in the section.
Following 5:90, this ayah names what gambling produces—enmity and hatred—and how it diverts people from God's remembrance and prayer.
The dead rush from their graves as though racing toward a nusub; the simile turns eagerness for the erected cult-stone into an image of resurrection and judgment.

Sacrificial camels are lined up with God's name pronounced, then their fallen sides yield food for the contented and the needy; this is the lawful counterpart to cutting a camel into chance-assigned shares.
The idolaters assign a nasib of crops and livestock to God and another to their partners; this exposes cultic apportionment itself rather than merely the objects worshipped.
Moses says rabbi ishrah li sadri, bringing Rabb, sharh, and sadr together in a prayer and making the section's three lexical strands meet in one address.
Moses then asks God to make his task easy, wa-yassir li amri; beside 20:25, ease is requested from the Lord rather than obtained from maysir.
The contenders cast their pens to determine who would care for Mary, a Qur'anic lot scene whose object and context differ sharply from gambling for meat.
Jonah participates in a drawing of lots and becomes one of those who lose; the ayah shows a lot selecting a person and an outcome rather than assigning cuts of a carcass.
God declares the water qismatun baynahum, an allotted division between the people and the she-camel, giving an animal-centered apportionment fixed by command rather than arrows.
They appoint a nasib from God's provision to beings they do not know, directly joining an assigned portion, provided goods, and false worship.
After describing what the people worship as inherited cult, God promises to pay them their nasib in full; worship and an undiminished allotted portion meet in the same ayah.
Inheritance gives both men and women nasiban mafruda, an obligatory appointed share; it is the clearest lawful counterpart to a portion won by arrows.
A debtor in hardship must be granted time until maysarah; this cognate of the section's y-s-r root makes ease an act of mercy in an economic relation, not the gain of maysir.
God's guidance is expressed as opening the breast for surrender, while misguidance makes it constricted; the ayah also ends with rijs, the term applied to the gambling-and-altars complex in 5:90.
The one whose breast God has opened to surrender stands in light from his Lord, repeating sharh and sadr while locating the opening with Rabb.
In the setting of restricted provision and measured spending, God promises to make ease after hardship; the share and the ease are divinely ordered rather than drawn by lot.
God explicitly desires yusr for people and not usr, identifying the giver and purpose of the ease whose root also names maysir.
The promise wa-nuyassiruka lil-yusra makes ease something God actively prepares for the addressee, matching the section's contrast with chance-drawn fortune.
People assign God a portion from His own servants, another idolatrous act of partition that parallels the cultic shares of livestock in 6:136.
Neither the sacrificial animals' flesh nor their blood reaches God; only mindfulness reaches Him, directly denying the efficacy imagined in blood poured upon a cult-stone.
The command to pray to your Lord and sacrifice directs both posture and slaughter to Rabb, reversing worship and killing at an erected stone.
Prayer, sacrifice, life, and death are declared wholly for God, Lord of the worlds, setting the proper recipient of ritual slaughter against the ansab.
Every community receives a rite so that God's name may be mentioned over the livestock He provided; provision, slaughter, and devotion are all returned to the one God.
At the appointed days God's name is spoken over provided livestock, after which people eat and feed the destitute; the meat is shared as worship and care rather than gambling.
The command to avoid rijs min al-awthan gives cult-images the same impurity language that 5:90 applies to maysir, ansab, and azlam.
The food boundary includes flowing blood and an animal sinfully dedicated to other than God; daman masfuhan sharply answers the section's blood poured over stones.
Eating is permitted where God's name has been mentioned, supplying the positive ritual boundary for the slaughter scene.
The prohibition on eating what lacks God's name identifies the decisive fault in cultic slaughter independently of how its meat is divided.
Blood and what has been dedicated to other than God are forbidden foods, a repeated boundary around the section's altar and carcass.
This repeated food law again joins blood with an animal dedicated to other than God, confirming that the sacrificial addressee governs the meat's status.
Sacrificial animals have benefits until an appointed term, but their proper destination is the Ancient House; the ayah replaces an arbitrary cult-stone with a divinely named place.
The two sons of Adam offer sacrifices, but acceptance belongs only to the mindful; ritual killing by itself therefore cannot secure a favorable outcome.
God ransoms Abraham's son with a great sacrifice, presenting slaughter as a divinely given release rather than a wager for portions.
Human formation clothes the bones with flesh; this reverses the section's dictionary image of sharh as flesh cut away from bones.
The resurrection sign raises the bones and then clothes them with flesh, another precise reversal of meat being stripped from bone.
A person who opens his breast to disbelief reverses the opening of the breast granted by God; the shared sharh-sadr construction marks the moral boundary.
The miserly denier is facilitated toward al-usra; paired with 92:7, the y-s-r root marks opposed moral destinations rather than luck at the arrows.
The idols worshipped besides God possess no provision, so the hearers are told to seek provision from God and worship Him; this directly counters seeking a share at cult objects.
After the naming of al-Lat, al-Uzza, and Manat and the assignment of daughters to God, the verdict tilka idhan qismatun diza condemns the cult's unequal division.
The named cult-figures are only names without divine authority, and their followers pursue conjecture and desire; this supplies the epistemic boundary for the arrows and their stones in 53:19-22.
God Himself instructs the heirs and fixes measured fractions for children and parents, replacing chance apportionment with an explicit legal division.
The remaining inheritance fractions are likewise fixed by divine instruction, extending the lawful model of an assigned share beyond the summary in 4:7.
The fifth of acquired spoils is assigned to named recipients by rule, providing another communal distribution governed by revelation rather than a draw.
The ban on consuming one another's wealth wrongfully, with mutually agreed trade as the stated alternative, locates gambling's transfer of wealth outside legitimate exchange.
The faces that are amilatun nasibah—laboring and exhausted—show that exertion by itself can end in fire; direction toward the Lord is what distinguishes the section's fanṣab.
Giving is the first act in the sequence that culminates in being facilitated toward ease at 92:7, opposing the acquisitive logic of gambling.
Affirming the best completes the moral posture that precedes facilitation toward ease in 92:7.
God says fa-sanuyassiruhu lil-yusra, making the easy way the prepared outcome of giving, fear, and truthfulness in 92:5-6.
Stinginess and self-sufficiency begin the contrary sequence completed by facilitation toward hardship in 92:10.
Denying the best supplies the moral cause paired with stinginess before the hard destination named in 92:10.
Whoever is mindful of God is promised yusran in the affair, another explicit case of ease being made by God.
Men and women each have a nasib from what they earn and are told to ask God for His bounty, linking apportioned benefit to effort and divine gift rather than a wager.
The instruction to give covenant partners their nasib presents a named, owed share within an ordered inheritance setting.
Each gate of Hell has a juzun maqsum, an assigned portion; the phrase shows apportionment as a fixed judgment rather than a lucky draw.
Abraham is told to prepare birds and place a portion on each mountain before they return alive; divided animal portions serve a resurrection sign rather than gain at play.
Thirst, nasab, and hunger suffered in God's path are credited as righteous action, giving concrete content to exertion directed toward the Lord.
God acknowledges that the Prophet's breast is constricted by hostile speech; 15:98 answers that constriction with praise and prostration to the Lord.
The command to glorify the Lord and prostrate answers the constricted breast in 15:97 and parallels the section's movement from bodily state to directed worship.
Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not flow, a negative state answered elsewhere by the prayer ishrah li sadri in 20:25.
The revealed Book is accompanied by the command that there be no constriction in the addressee's breast, supplying the boundary opposite sharh al-sadr.
Qum al-layla commands bodily rising for worship, a close nonlexical parallel to the section's upright exertion after becoming free.
Remembering the Lord's name and devoting oneself wholly to Him states the direction of the exertion that the section contrasts with standing before a stone.
Qum fa-andhir turns rising into a commanded task, while the next ayah identifies the Lord as the one to magnify.
Wa-rabbaka fa-kabbir directs the risen addressee of 74:2 toward his Lord, matching the paired imperatives in 94:7-8.
Abraham asks why his people remain devoted before their statues; their bodily devotion to objects clarifies the section's contrast with turning toward Rabb.
The people say they worship idols and remain devoted to them, staging sustained attendance before cult objects rather than devotion to the Lord.
Abraham asks whether they worship what they carve, making the manufactured material object in the section's erected-stone scene explicit.
The naming of al-Lat and al-Uzza begins the concrete Arabian cult setting whose allocation is condemned as an unjust division in 53:22.
Manat, the third named cult-figure, completes the set immediately before the passage exposes the worshippers' biased apportionment.
The question assigning males to the hearers and females to God states the two sides of the division judged unjust in 53:22.
The command to leave them plunging and playing until the promised day leads directly into their rush toward a nusub-like goal in 70:43, turning heedless play toward judgment.
Downcast eyes and enveloping humiliation complete the resurrection rush of 70:43 and disclose the end of their former eagerness toward the erected object.
The invented categories of consecrated livestock—bahirah, sa'ibah, wasilah, and ham—extend the section's pre-Islamic animal-and-cult setting and identify it as a fabrication against God.
Continuing the cultic shares of 6:136, this ayah reports livestock and crops reserved by claim, animals whose use was forbidden, and animals over which God's name was withheld.
The contents of certain animals' wombs are assigned to men, denied to wives, and shared if born dead; it is a precise cultic allocation of animal flesh by invented rules.

A deliberately killed game animal requires an equivalent livestock offering assessed by two just people and brought to the Kaaba, replacing chance division with measured judgment and a named destination.
The she-camel has one drinking share and the people another on a known day, a repeated animal-centered apportionment fixed in advance rather than drawn by arrows.
God says that the treasuries of all things are with Him and that He sends each down only in a known measure, locating hidden provision and its portion with God.
God sends provision in due measure because unrestricted abundance would provoke transgression; the ayah gives a reason for divinely measured shares.
God provides from an unexpected source and has set a measure for everything, directly opposing the attempt to secure one's portion through a random draw.
People are challenged for turning God's provision into lawful and forbidden portions without authorization, a boundary against humanly invented rules for food.
Those worshipped apart from God possess no provision for their worshippers, exposing the futility of seeking a material share through cult objects.
God fixes the sibling shares in the final inheritance ruling and says He makes the law clear, another explicit alternative to allocation by chance.
Alms are assigned to named recipient groups as an obligation from God, presenting communal goods as a divinely fixed distribution.
When asked about spoils, the hearers are told that they belong to God and the Messenger and must repair relations and obey, placing contested goods under revelation rather than a wager.
Public wealth is assigned to named recipients so that it does not circulate only among the rich, giving both a rule and an ethical purpose for distribution.
The people of the Garden will not be touched by nasab, marking freedom from exhaustion as the final boundary of the present command to exert oneself.
The inhabitants of the lasting abode praise God because neither toil nor weariness touches them there; nasab belongs to the journey, not its divinely granted end.
The command qumu lillahi qanitin makes standing an act performed devoutly for God, sharply distinguishing sacred posture from attendance at an erected stone.
The night worshipper alternates prostration and standing while fearing the Hereafter and hoping for the Lord's mercy, showing upright exertion directed by knowledge and hope.
The servants of the Merciful spend the night prostrating and standing for their Lord, a sustained bodily counter-image to devotion before a cult-stone.
The Prophet is forbidden ever to stand in the harmful mosque and told that a mosque founded on mindfulness is worthier for standing, making the place and object of upright worship morally decisive.
Sacrificial animals and their garlands are declared inviolable signs on the way to the Sacred House, supplying a sanctioned ritual-animal setting opposite the ansab.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are designated supports for people, identifying the divinely ordered center and objects of sacrifice.
The sacrificial offering must reach its appointed place before release from consecration, so the animal has a prescribed destination rather than an erected pagan stone.
Sacrificial animals are described as prevented from reaching their proper place, confirming that lawful offerings have a recognized destination.

Between the livestock shares of 6:136 and the invented restrictions of 6:138, the partners make killing children seem fair and thereby confuse the people's religion; it states the destructive power of the same cultic authority.
God's messenger identifies the she-camel as God's and protects her drinking share, a compressed parallel to the apportioned camel-and-water scene.
The Lord expands provision for whom He wills and measures it, locating both abundance and restriction in His knowledge rather than fortune.
Dhul-Qarnayn promises the righteous a good reward and an easy word from his command, using ease in the act of assigning a just outcome.
The person given the record in the right hand receives an easy reckoning, making ease a judged outcome rather than a lucky allotment.
Those who invent lies against God receive the portion appointed for them in the Book until death overtakes them; a fixed nasib answers their false cult claims.
The hearer is told to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting his nasib of worldly life, joining divine gift to a bounded personal portion.
The seeker of worldly harvest is granted some of it but has no nasib in the Hereafter, showing that the lasting share turns on one's chosen aim rather than chance.
Between the God-named livestock of 22:34 and the camel sacrifice of 22:36, this ayah defines the humble worshippers as patient, prayerful, and generous from God's provision.
